title: What the venue owner adds to our keyword research

content.job: Standalone list email telling the full exchange and the collaboration principle. No offer, result claim or reply request; proposed send metadata requires WIA confirmation.
content.body:
Our team had brought the existing keywords and some proposed additions to the conversation. She explained that the shortened name was familiar to local people, as well as some couples coming from outside the area. If couples use a name like that when they talk about the area, some may use it when they search, and a keyword list put together from outside the market can miss a term like that.

The team agreed to look into her suggestion and share any additional terms they found.

It was a small exchange, but it illustrates something we value in an advertising partnership. Our team contributed the recommendations and the commitment to research. The client contributed context about how people talk about her market.

**Your firsthand knowledge of couples deserves a place alongside our advertising expertise.**

When you're already investing in Google Ads, you want the people supporting you to bring considered recommendations. You also have knowledge built through the conversations you're having with people who might choose your venue.

Those contributions can work together. The person speaking with couples can offer context that's useful to the team researching how to reach them.

We believe a recommendation should give us something meaningful to discuss with you. There should be room for your experience to contribute while we're considering the strategy, with our team taking responsibility for investigating the questions that arise.
content.ending:
If you've ever wondered where your own read on couples fits once you hire help with Google Ads, this is how we'd want it to work: our research in front of you, and room for what you know.

Talk soon,
Whitney

slides.job: State the promise as an insight about the reader.

What you hear from couples belongs in your Google Ads strategy.

You hire specialists for their advertising expertise.
The way couples describe your area is something you know firsthand, and **it's worth bringing into the keyword conversation.**

slides.job: Establish the team's contribution and invitation.
slides.text:
In a review with a venue client, we walked through her current Google keywords and the additions we were recommending.

While those recommendations were still being considered, we invited her questions and concerns about the list.

slides.job: Credit the client's contribution without identifying the market.
slides.text:
She raised the shortened name people use for the region.

slides.job: Show the team's response, stopping at the evidenced commitment.
slides.text:
We said we'd research it and send her any other terms we turned up.

slides.job: Connect the exchange to an owner who already advertises.
slides.text:
If you're advertising your venue, you have something to bring to this.

You talk with people deciding whether to get married in your area.
You hear how they describe the location and how familiar it is to them.

slides.job: Explain how the two contributions complement each other.
slides.text:
Our side is a researched starting point: the keywords, the recommendations and the reasoning behind them.

Your side is context we can't see from where we sit.
Each does a different job in the same conversation.

slides.job: State WIA's belief without turning one exchange into a claim about every call.
slides.text:
**We believe the person closest to your couples should have a voice in your keyword research.**

The way couples talk can help inform what we explore, while the advertising expertise and the research stay with our team.

slides.job: Deepen the distinction between contributing context and supplying a finished recommendation.
slides.text:
You don't need to arrive with a finished campaign idea.

Telling us what you hear is enough to start.
In this case, the client pointed to something worth a look, and the research became ours to do.

slides.job: Close for both management and guided-launch readers without an explicit CTA.
slides.text:
Whether you want our team to manage your ads, or to launch your campaigns and guide you while you run them, what you know about your couples belongs in the partnership.

We want our expertise working with it.

caption.body:
When you already market your venue, you spend a lot of time with the couples considering it. You hear how they talk about the area, what they call it and how well they know it. And when you bring in advertising specialists, you want that experience to count for something.

A keyword discussion with a venue client gives a small example. We reviewed the terms already in place and our proposed additions, then invited her perspective. She brought up the abbreviation locals use for the region and described how familiar it is to some couples visiting from elsewhere.

We agreed to investigate and pass along anything further we found. The client contributed the context, and our team committed to the research.

The value of that conversation reaches past the suggestion itself. It shows how a prepared recommendation can turn into a useful discussion with someone who knows the market firsthand.

Owners who invest in specialist support should be able to bring that experience in while the strategy is being considered, with a clear role for the expertise on each side.
caption.hook: Being asked to approve a Google keyword list is different from being invited to add to it.
caption.ending: In this review, that meant our recommendations on the table, her suggestion about a local name, and our team agreeing to look into it.

content.title: Reel 1: the local name she raised in her keyword review
content.script:
A venue client gave our team another phrase to investigate for her Google Ads.

Here's what happened. Our team was reviewing the keywords she already had, along with some additional recommendations. And they asked whether she had any questions or concerns about the list.

She brought up the shorthand people use for her area. She explained that local people use it, and some couples from outside the area do, too. And if couples say it, some of them might be searching it, too. And that's exactly the kind of term that's easy to miss when the list is built from the outside.

Our team said they'd look into it and share any other terms they found.

What stands out to me is how she contributed. She brought something she knew about the way people talk about her market into the research conversation.

When you're speaking with couples, you're hearing language that can be useful to the people working on your ads. We bring our advertising expertise, and you bring that firsthand experience.

I think a good partnership should give both a place in the strategy, so your knowledge of couples can help shape what our team explores.

caption.body:
If you're paying for Google Ads, you want specialists who bring a considered recommendation to the table. You also have knowledge of your market that comes from speaking directly with the people choosing a wedding venue.

Those contributions can work together. During a keyword review, our team asked a venue client for questions about the existing terms and the additions being proposed. She suggested looking into a familiar abbreviation for her area, explaining that people used it locally and that it was familiar to some couples traveling in, too. If couples use a name like that in conversation, some may use it when they search.

Our team agreed to research the suggestion and share any further terms they found. Her contribution gave the team another question to pursue.

We believe that kind of exchange belongs in an advertising partnership. The research gives the conversation a starting point, while the client's experience can add something worth exploring. For an owner who already knows the market well, expert support should offer a useful place for that knowledge.

caption.ending:
What you hear from couples can give our team something worth researching, and the digging stays with us.

-Whitney

content.title: Reel 2: starting with the keywords already in her account
content.script:
When a venue already has Google Ads running, what happens to the keywords that are in there?

That was the situation with one of our venue clients. Her ads were already running when our team sat down with her Google keywords. So the first thing they did was make a note of the current terms in the account. And our team thought those terms were good.

So the recommendations were built around them. The new keywords were meant to level up what was already in there, and the team kept the total focused, probably somewhere around 10 to 15 keywords.

Then they put the whole list in front of her, the current terms and the new ones side by side, and asked how it looked.

When you bring a new team into your Google Ads, the work already in your account doesn't have to be thrown out. I think a careful review starts with what's there, and then decides what to add on purpose.

caption.body:
If you've been advertising your venue, your Google account isn't a blank page. There are keywords in there already, and when you bring in specialists, it's fair to wonder what they'll do with them.

In this venue's review, our team began with that list. Ads were already running, so the existing terms were recorded first, and the team considered them good. The recommended additions were then shaped to sit alongside them, with the total kept to a focused number, probably around 10 to 15 keywords.

The client then saw the established terms and the new ones together in one list, and was asked how the combined list looked.

In this review, the starting point was a positive assessment of the existing terms. Those keywords gave our team something real to assess, and the additions were presented in relation to them. In this account, the team had useful terms to discuss before bringing additional ones into consideration.

caption.body:
You already know the parts of your venue couples can't find just anywhere. The question for your Google Ads is whether those same things show up in what people search for.

For one venue client, that was the all-inclusive offering. During her Google keyword review, our team pointed to it as a real point of difference, and the suggestions included language about all-inclusive venues and wedding packages. It was an option she offered, and someone searching for it intentionally could be looking for that kind of wedding arrangement.

A distinctive offer was only part of the picture. Our team also discussed search volume, cost and competition, and those considerations came with the recommendations, so the client was looking at the reasoning as well as a list of phrases.

Here, the all-inclusive offering gave our team a specific direction to explore and explain to the client.
